lessons.title: Entering an uneven cash-flow stream
lessons.intro: Your company is weighing a machine that costs $7,000 today. The forecast says it will bring in $3,000 the first year, $5,000 a year in years 2 through 5, and $4,000 in year 6. The amounts change from year to year, so this is a job for the Cash Flow worksheet, not TVM.

steps.explain: Press CF to open the Cash Flow worksheet, then 2ND CLR WORK to wipe any flows left over from earlier work. The display lands on CFo, the cash flow at time zero, at its default of 0.

The $7,000 purchase price is money leaving your pocket, so key the amount, press +/- to flip its sign, then ENTER to store it. The rule for the whole worksheet: money you receive is positive, money you pay out is negative.
Arrow down to C01, the first cash flow after time zero, and store the $3,000 the machine earns in year 1. It comes to you, so it stays positive.
Arrow down again and F01 appears: how many years in a row C01 repeats. It already reads 1, the default, which is exactly right for a single year, so there is nothing to key.
Move on to C02 and enter $5,000, the amount expected in each of years 2 through 5.
Years 2 through 5 are four identical amounts in a row, so instead of typing 5,000 four times, set the frequency F02 to 4. One slot now covers all four years.
Move to C03 and enter the $4,000 expected in year 6.
F03 shows the default frequency of 1, correct for the single year 6. Seven years of cash flows now fit in just three slots.

lessons.answer: The stream is stored: CFo = -7,000; C01 = 3,000 (once); C02 = 5,000 (4 times); C03 = 4,000 (once). Keeping outflows negative and inflows positive is what makes the NPV and IRR you compute later mean anything.

lessons.title: Fixing a stream with delete and insert
lessons.intro: You entered a stream of -7,000 now, 3,000 in year 1, 5,000 in years 2-5, and 4,000 in year 6 — then the forecast changes: the $4,000 actually arrives in year 2, pushing the four $5,000 years back to years 3-6. Rather than retype everything, fix it with one delete and one insert.

steps.explain: Open the Cash Flow worksheet, clear it, and store the initial -7,000. Negative, because the purchase price is money you pay out.
Store 3,000 as C01, the year-1 inflow.
Press down twice to skip past F01 — it stays at its default of 1 — and store 5,000 at C02.
Set F02 to 4, grouping the four consecutive $5,000 years into one slot.
Store 4,000 at C03. The original, soon-to-be-corrected stream is now fully in place.
Step down to glance at F03 and back up to C03, the flow we want to remove. Delete acts on whichever cash flow is on the display, so parking the display on C03 first is the whole trick.
2ND DEL removes the displayed cash flow — the amount and its frequency go together, and any later flows slide down a slot. C03 now reads 0.00 because the list just got one group shorter.
Two presses of up walk back through F02 to C02. The corrected $4,000 belongs here, in year 2.
2ND INS opens a brand-new slot right here at C02, pushing the old C02 and everything after it up one number. Key 4,000 and ENTER to fill the new slot.
The inserted flow arrives with the default frequency of 1 — you never keyed it.
Arrow down to confirm the displaced 5,000 now lives at C03.
And its frequency of 4 travelled with it to F03. When flows shift, an amount and its frequency always move as a pair.

lessons.answer: The edited stream reads CFo = -7,000; C01 = 3,000; C02 = 4,000; C03 = 5,000 (4 times) — corrected with one delete and one insert instead of retyping the whole list.

lessons.title: Computing net present value at 20%
lessons.intro: A $7,000 machine is expected to return $3,000 in year 1, $4,000 in year 2, and $5,000 a year in years 3 through 6. Your company only takes projects that earn at least 20% a year. Compute the net present value to see whether this one clears the bar.

steps.explain: Open and clear the Cash Flow worksheet, then store the $7,000 cost as a negative CFo — it is money paid out today.
Store the year-1 inflow of 3,000 at C01.
Skip past F01, leaving it at its default of 1, and store the year-2 inflow of 4,000 at C02.
Skip past F02 the same way and store 5,000 at C03 — the amount for each of years 3 through 6.
Set F03 to 4 so the single C03 slot covers all four $5,000 years.
Press NPV. The display does not jump to an answer — it opens I, the discount rate, at 0. This I belongs to the Cash Flow worksheet and is completely separate from the TVM worksheet's I/Y.
Enter 20, the required return. The rate is a percent per cash-flow period — here the periods are years, so the 20% annual target goes in as-is.
Arrow down to the NPV variable and press CPT. The calculator discounts every future flow back to today at 20% and nets them against the -7,000.

lessons.answer: NPV = 7,266.44 — in today's dollars the stream is worth $7,266.44 more than the machine costs, even after demanding 20% a year. A positive NPV means the project clears the hurdle; take it.

lessons.title: Computing the internal rate of return
lessons.intro: Same machine as the NPV lesson: $7,000 out today, then $3,000, $4,000, and four years of $5,000 coming back. Instead of testing the stream against a 20% target, ask it directly: what annual rate does this investment actually earn?

steps.explain: Open and clear the Cash Flow worksheet and store the initial outflow of -7,000. The one negative flow up front matters: IRR needs the stream to change sign at least once.
Store the year-1 inflow of 3,000 at C01.
Skip F01 (it stays at 1) and store the year-2 inflow of 4,000 at C02.
Skip F02 and store 5,000 at C03 for years 3 through 6.
Set F03 to 4 to cover the four $5,000 years in one slot.
Press IRR. It opens showing 0.00 — nothing has been solved yet. Notice you never supply a discount rate: the rate is exactly what IRR goes hunting for.
CPT starts an iterative search for the rate that makes the stream's net present value exactly zero. On long streams this can take a moment.

lessons.answer: IRR = 52.71 — the investment earns 52.71% a year; discounted at that rate, the inflows exactly repay the $7,000. Because the stream flips sign only once (money out, then only money in), this rate is the only one that works — no second answer exists.

lessons.title: Pricing a lease with a monthly discount rate
lessons.intro: A 36-month equipment lease, payable at the start of each month, charges nothing in months 1-4, $5,000 in months 5-12, nothing in months 13-15, $6,000 in months 16-24, nothing in months 25-26, and $7,000 in months 27-36. What is that whole obligation worth today, discounted at 10% a year?

steps.explain: Start from a completely clean slate: 2ND RESET ENTER restores every variable in the calculator to its default, so nothing left over can leak into this problem.

Open the Cash Flow worksheet. Payments fall at the beginning of each month, and this worksheet has no BGN/END switch — instead, the month-1 payment simply becomes CFo. Month 1 costs $0, so CFo stays at 0.
Arrow down to C01, which covers the remaining free months. Leave the amount at its 0 default — stepping past a slot keeps whatever it already holds.
Set F01 to 3 for months 2-4. Only three, not four: month 1 of the free stretch was already used up by CFo.
The $5,000 payments leave your pocket, so key 5000, press +/- to make it negative, and ENTER. Every payment in this lease is an outflow.
Eight months at $5,000 (months 5-12). Grouping with frequencies is what lets a 36-month lease fit the worksheet's 24 slots.
Step past C03, leaving it at 0 for the free months 13-15, and set its frequency to 3. A $0 group still needs its own slot — it has to occupy its place on the timeline.
Months 16-24 cost $6,000 each: another negative entry.
Nine months at that amount.
Step past C05 — free months again — and set its frequency to 2 for months 25-26.
The final stretch costs $7,000 a month. Negative again.
Ten months at $7,000 completes the timeline: 1 + 3 + 8 + 3 + 9 + 2 + 10 = 36 months.
Press NPV to reach the discount rate I, sitting at 0.

The flows are monthly but 10% is a yearly rate, and this worksheet never converts rates for you. Key 10 ÷ 12 and press ENTER: the calculator does the division on the spot and stores the result. The display rounds to 0.83, but the stored monthly rate keeps its full precision — that is what makes the final answer come out right.
Arrow down to NPV and press CPT to discount all 36 months back to today.

lessons.answer: NPV = -138,088.44 — signing this lease is equivalent to paying $138,088.44 in cash today. The answer is negative because every flow is money out; it is a price tag, not a verdict, and you would compare it against other ways of financing the same equipment.
